meta.blurb: In 1764 a young Englishman sat among the ruins of Rome, listened to friars singing on the Capitol, and decided to learn how it all fell. Edward Gibbon follows the story for over a thousand years, to the fall of Constantinople.
meta.bible: Edward Gibbon: English historian, born 1737, died 1794. In October 1764 he sat among the ruins of the Capitol in Rome while friars sang in a church on the site of the old temple of Jupiter, and the idea of the book came to him. His History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire was published in six volumes between 1776 and 1788; he finished it on 27 June 1787 in a summer-house in his garden at Lausanne, in Switzerland. It covers about thirteen hundred years, from the second century AD to the fall of Constantinople in 1453. His famous view: the empire fell partly because it grew too big, 'immoderate greatness', and because soldiers, money and new beliefs changed it; he also suggested natural causes for the rise of Christianity, which offended many believers. Historians still debate his causes, and many now prefer to speak of a slow change rather than a sudden fall. Emperors: Trajan (reigned 98 to 117, the empire at its widest), Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius (died 180), Commodus (murdered 192), Didius Julianus (bought the throne in 193), Valerian (captured by the Persians in 260), Aurelian (reunited the empire, built the Aurelian Walls), Diocletian (reigned 284 to 305, retired to Split), Constantine (won at the Milvian Bridge in 312, ruled alone from 324, founded Constantinople in 330, died 337), Julian (361 to 363), Valens (killed 378), Theodosius (died 395), Honorius, Romulus Augustulus (deposed in 476), Justinian (527 to 565, law code and Hagia Sophia), Heraclius (610 to 641), Constantine the Eleventh (died defending Constantinople in 1453). Empress Theodora: Justinian's wife. Others: Stilicho (Roman general, executed 408), Alaric (Gothic king, sacked Rome in 410), Gaiseric (king of the Vandals, took Carthage in 439, sacked Rome in 455), Attila (king of the Huns, stopped in Gaul in 451, met Pope Leo in 452, died 453), Odoacer (German officer who deposed Romulus in 476), Belisarius (Justinian's general), Muhammad (died 632), Charlemagne (crowned emperor in Rome on Christmas Day in the year 800), Mehmed the Second (Ottoman sultan, took Constantinople on 29 May 1453), Poggio Bracciolini (Italian scholar who looked on the ruins of Rome in the 1430s). Places and groups: Rome, Constantinople (now Istanbul), Byzantium, Danube, Adrianople (battle of 378), Carthage, Ravenna, Persia, the Sassanid kings, Goths, Visigoths, Vandals, Huns, Franks, Arabs, Turks, Ottomans, Venice, the Praetorian Guard, the Tetrarchy, the Aurelian Walls, Hagia Sophia, the Golden Horn. Key terms: Empire, Senate, Legion, Barbarian, Pagan, Crusade, Plague. Dates are AD unless stated; numbers are about unless exact. Voice and tone: calm, clear and a little wry, like a great storyteller who is honest about what is disputed; religion is treated respectfully and neutrally; violence is stated plainly with no gore.

B1B2: In October 1764 a young Englishman named Edward Gibbon sat among the ruins of ancient Rome while friars sang in a church nearby. He asked himself how such a great city had fallen, and he decided to write the answer.

Gibbon wrote six large volumes, which appeared between 1776 and 1788. They follow the story of Rome for about thirteen hundred years, from the empire at its height to the fall of Constantinople in 1453.
In about the year 117, under the emperor Trajan, the Roman Empire reached its greatest size. It stretched from Britain in the north-west to Syria in the east, and surrounded the Mediterranean Sea.

Gibbon thought that the years from 96 to 180 were the happiest in history, though many people were poor or enslaved. In that time a series of capable emperors each chose a skilled successor by adopting him.
The army, the roads, the laws and the towns held the empire together. A traveller could cross thousands of miles on good roads, and Roman law protected most free people, wherever they lived.
The thoughtful emperor Marcus Aurelius died in 180, and for the first time in many years, his own son took the throne. The son, Commodus, was cruel and lazy, and he was murdered in 192.

In 193 the soldiers of the Praetorian Guard killed an emperor, and, according to ancient writers, they offered the throne for sale. A rich senator named Didius Julianus paid the most, but he ruled for only a few weeks.

In the third century the empire was torn by civil wars, and many generals fought to become emperor. More than twenty emperors ruled in about fifty years, and most of them were killed by their own soldiers.
In 260 the Persian king Shapur defeated the Roman army and captured the emperor Valerian. It was a terrible shock, because no Roman emperor had ever been taken alive by an enemy before.
The emperor Aurelian won back the lost provinces and, by 274, had reunited the empire. He also built a strong new wall around the city of Rome, which shows that even Rome now felt in danger.
Diocletian became emperor in 284, and he decided that the empire was too big for one man to rule. He shared power with three others, and he also reformed the taxes and the army.
In 305 Diocletian did something very rare for an emperor, and retired. He went to his palace by the sea at Split, where, according to the story, he enjoyed growing vegetables.

In 312 Constantine defeated a rival at the Milvian Bridge, near Rome, and he became the master of the western empire. He said that he had seen a sign in the sky, and the next year he gave Christians the freedom to worship.

Gibbon wrote about how Christianity grew from a small group into the main religion of the empire. He listed natural reasons, such as the courage of believers and their care for each other, and some readers were offended.
In 330 Constantine opened a new capital city on the narrow strait between Europe and Asia. It was called Constantinople, and it was well placed, rich and easy to defend.
After Constantine died, his family fought one another for power. In 361 his nephew Julian became emperor, and he tried to bring back the old gods, but he died in battle against Persia in 363.

In 376 thousands of Goths came to the Danube, because the fierce Huns had driven them from their homes. They asked the Romans to let them cross the river, and the Romans agreed, but they treated the Goths badly.
In 378 the Gothic armies met the Roman emperor Valens at Adrianople, and they won a great victory. Valens was killed, and two-thirds of his army may have been lost.
Theodosius made peace with the Goths and was the last emperor to rule the whole empire. When he died in 395, his two young sons shared it, one in the east and one in the west.
The Roman general Stilicho defended Italy against the Gothic king Alaric for many years. But the weak western emperor Honorius turned against him, and in 408 Stilicho was put to death.
In 410 Alaric and his Goths entered Rome, and they stayed for three days. It was the first time in almost eight hundred years that an enemy had taken the city, and it shocked the whole Roman world.
The Vandals crossed the Rhine in 406 and travelled through Gaul and Spain. In 429 they sailed to Africa, and in 439 their king Gaiseric took Carthage, one of the richest cities in the west.
Attila, the king of the Huns, led a huge army into Gaul in 451. A Roman general named Aetius joined with the Goths and stopped him at a great battle on the Catalaunian Plains.
In 452 Attila invaded Italy, and Pope Leo went to meet him, and Attila turned back. In 455 the Vandals reached Rome from the sea, and they plundered the city for about two weeks.
In 476 a German officer named Odoacer removed the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus. Odoacer did not choose a new emperor, and most historians mark this as the end of the western empire.
Gibbon thought that Rome fell mostly because of its own greatness. In his view, success made the empire too large and too dependent on its soldiers, so it was slowly weakened from inside.

Gibbon also blamed the power of the army and the loss of public spirit among the citizens. He thought that the rise of a new religion, with its focus on a life after death, had made people less interested in public life.
While the west fell, the eastern half of the empire survived, with its capital at Constantinople. In 527 an energetic emperor named Justinian took the throne, together with his clever wife Theodora.
Justinian had the old Roman laws collected and arranged into one great code. He also built the huge church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, which was finished in 537.
Justinian's general Belisarius won back North Africa from the Vandals and parts of Italy from the Goths. In 541, however, a terrible plague began, and it killed a large part of the population.
In the early seventh century Rome and Persia fought a long and costly war. Heraclius, the Roman emperor, finally defeated the Persians in 627, but both empires were left exhausted.
Muhammad, the founder of Islam, died in 632, and Arab armies then moved out of Arabia with astonishing speed. Within a few years they had taken Syria, Jerusalem and Egypt from the Roman Empire.
Gibbon wrote at length about Muhammad and the early Muslim conquests. He tried to be fair, which was unusual among European writers of his time, and he praised some of the early caliphs.

On Christmas Day in the year 800, Pope Leo the Third crowned Charlemagne, the king of the Franks, as emperor in Rome. The emperors in Constantinople were not pleased, because they believed that they were the true Romans.

Gibbon often described the later Byzantine court as full of plots, cruelty and empty ceremony. Many modern historians think that he was unfair, and that the Byzantines kept learning, art and law alive.
In 1071 the Seljuk Turks defeated the Byzantine army, and the empire lost much of Anatolia. The emperor asked the Christians in the west for help, and this led to the Crusades.

In 1204 the Fourth Crusade, led by Venice and the Crusaders, attacked Constantinople instead of going to the Holy Land. They captured the city, plundered it for three days, and the empire never fully recovered.
In 1261 the Byzantines took Constantinople back, but the city was damaged and the empire was much smaller. The emperor ruled over only a few lands, and enemies were close on every side.

From about 1300, the Ottoman Turks grew stronger and took one Byzantine land after another. Their sultan Bayezid nearly took Constantinople, but in 1402 a great conqueror named Timur defeated him and the city was spared for a while.

The young sultan Mehmed the Second came to power in 1451, and he was determined to take Constantinople. He built a fortress beside the strait, and he hired a cannon maker named Urban to cast huge guns.

The siege of Constantinople began in April 1453, and the defenders were few, perhaps one tenth as many as the Ottomans. They stretched a chain across the harbour, and the Ottomans answered by dragging ships overland.
Before dawn on 29 May 1453, the Ottomans made a final attack, and this time they broke through. Most accounts say that the last emperor, Constantine the Eleventh, died fighting in the streets.

After the conquest, Mehmed made Constantinople his capital, and the great church of Hagia Sophia became a mosque. With that, the long story of Rome, which tradition said had begun more than two thousand years earlier, came to an end.
Gibbon ended his book by returning to the ruins of Rome. He remembered how an Italian scholar named Poggio had sat among them in the 1430s and thought about how fortune turns.
Gibbon finished writing late on the night of 27 June 1787, in a summer-house in his garden at Lausanne. He felt joy that the work was done, but also sadness that he had to say goodbye to it.
The first volume appeared in 1776, and it quickly sold out. The last three volumes appeared in 1788, and by then Gibbon was one of the most famous writers in Europe.
Some churchmen attacked Gibbon for what he had written about early Christianity. He answered his critics in a pamphlet, which was published in 1779, but he did not change his mind.
Later scholars have found errors in Gibbon, and they know much more about the ancient world than he did. But they still admire how carefully he read the ancient sources.

Many historians today prefer to say that the Roman world changed slowly instead of falling suddenly. Roman law, language and religion lived on in new kingdoms, and the eastern empire lasted for nearly a thousand years after 476.
Gibbon died in January 1794, at the age of fifty-six, but his book is still read more than two centuries later. It reminds us that even great powers can be weakened by their own success.
C1C2: One evening in October 1764, a young Englishman named Edward Gibbon sat among the broken columns of the Capitol in Rome, while friars sang their evening prayers in a church built where the temple of Jupiter had once stood. The contrast between the proud past and the silent ruins struck him so deeply that he began to wonder how the greatest empire in the world had come to this. The idea that formed in his mind that evening would occupy him, on and off, for most of the next twenty-three years.

Gibbon laboured for the better part of two decades on a work in six large volumes, published between 1776 and 1788, which he called the History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire. It follows the story from the empire at the height of its power in the second century all the way down to the fall of Constantinople in 1453, covering some thirteen hundred years. Few historians before or since have attempted so wide a canvas, and fewer still have painted it with such confidence.

In about the year 117, in the reign of the emperor Trajan, the Roman Empire reached the greatest extent it would ever know, stretching from the cold hills of northern Britain to the deserts of Syria and Egypt. Its provinces encircled the Mediterranean Sea so completely that the Romans could fairly call it their own lake, and its people spoke Latin in the west and Greek in the east. It was an astonishing achievement of conquest, organisation and government, and everything that follows in Gibbon's story is measured against it.

Gibbon famously wrote that if anyone were asked to name the time in history when the human race was most prosperous and happy, he would choose the years from 96 to 180, though many people in that world were poor or enslaved. In those years five able emperors succeeded one another, and most of them chose a capable successor by adopting him rather than leaving the throne to a son. Gibbon admired this system, which for almost a century gave the empire good rulers and long peace.

Several things kept so vast a territory together: a professional army camped on the frontiers, a network of excellent roads, a single body of law, and hundreds of towns that copied the habits of Rome. A traveller could journey for thousands of miles in safety, using the same coins and meeting the same kind of magistrate. Gibbon saw this orderly world as a remarkable achievement, but he also suspected that its very success contained the seeds of future weakness.

The wise and thoughtful emperor Marcus Aurelius, who had spent much of his reign fighting on the northern frontier, died in the year 180. Unlike his predecessors, he left the throne to his own son Commodus, a vain, cruel and lazy young man who preferred performing as a gladiator to governing. Commodus ruled for about twelve years before his own household murdered him, and Gibbon regards his death as the point at which the empire's good fortune began to run out.

In the year 193, after the soldiers of the Praetorian Guard had murdered Commodus's successor, they are said by ancient writers to have offered the throne to the highest bidder. A wealthy senator named Didius Julianus paid a fortune for the honour, but he was executed after only a few weeks when rival generals marched on Rome. Gibbon points to this shameful episode as proof that the real power in the empire now rested with the army.

The third century was a time of turmoil, in which generals were made emperor by their legions, and then were murdered by the very men who had proclaimed them. More than twenty men claimed the throne in about fifty years, and at the same time the empire suffered from foreign invasions, plague and rising prices. Gibbon describes the whole sorry procession of soldiers' emperors as a lesson in what happens when force replaces law.

In 260 the great Persian king Shapur defeated a Roman army in the east and took the emperor Valerian prisoner, an event that sent a shudder through the whole empire. No Roman emperor had ever before fallen alive into the hands of a foreign enemy, and Valerian never returned home. Meanwhile, parts of the empire in the west and in the east broke away under their own rulers, and the old unity of the Roman world seemed to be in pieces.

The soldier-emperor Aurelian was the first to turn the tide, defeating the breakaway rulers of the east and the west, and by 274 he had put the empire together again. He also surrounded Rome with a massive brick wall, much of which still stands today, and the fact that the capital needed such protection says a great deal about how the times had changed. For the first time in centuries, the heart of the empire felt itself within reach of its enemies.

Diocletian, who became emperor in 284, understood that the empire was too large for any one man to defend, and so he divided the rule among four men, two senior and two junior, in a system called the Tetrarchy. He reorganised the provinces, raised taxes to pay a larger army, and demanded that his subjects treat him with the ceremony of a king. Gibbon admired his skill but thought that his court, with its cost and its ritual, was a step away from the old, simple Roman state.

In the year 305, after more than twenty years in power, Diocletian did something almost unheard of among Roman emperors, which was to retire willingly. He withdrew to a vast palace that he had built on the Adriatic coast at Split, in what is now Croatia, and later tradition says that he took more pleasure in growing cabbages than in ruling. The arrangement he left behind collapsed in civil war almost as soon as he stepped aside.

In 312 Constantine defeated his rival Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge just outside Rome, and he claimed afterward that a heavenly sign had promised him victory. A year later he and his fellow ruler issued a statement allowing Christians to practise their religion freely after years of persecution, and in 324 he became sole ruler of the whole empire. Historians still argue about how deeply Constantine believed, but few doubt that his reign changed the world.

In two famous chapters, Gibbon asked how a small and often persecuted group had grown into the main faith of the empire, and he looked for explanations that belonged to ordinary human history. He pointed to the zeal and courage of the early believers, their hope of life after death, their strict morals and their well-organised communities, and he treated these as natural causes. Many Christian readers were angered that a historian should explain so sacred a story without mentioning divine help, and the dispute followed him all his life.

In 330 Constantine dedicated a new capital on the site of the old Greek town of Byzantium, where Europe and Asia almost touch across a narrow strait. The city, named Constantinople in his honour, stood on a triangle of land that was easy to defend, close to the frontiers and in command of the sea routes between the Mediterranean and the Black Sea. It would remain the capital of the eastern empire for more than eleven hundred years, long after Rome itself had fallen.

After Constantine's death in 337, his sons quarrelled and fought, and in 361 the throne passed to his clever nephew Julian, a scholar who had secretly turned away from Christianity. Julian tried to restore the old gods and to reduce the privileges of the Church, but his reign was short, and he was mortally wounded in 363 while fighting the Persians. Gibbon, who found Julian a fascinating and complicated man, treats his failure as proof that the old religion could not be revived.

In 376 a huge multitude of Goths gathered on the northern bank of the Danube, driven from their homes by the Huns, a warlike people from the distant steppes. They begged the Roman authorities to let them settle inside the empire, and the emperor, hoping for soldiers and taxpayers, agreed. Roman officials, however, cheated and mistreated them, and the starving refugees soon turned from supplicants into enemies.

In 378 the Roman emperor Valens marched out to fight the Goths near Adrianople, in what is now north-western Turkey, and was destroyed with most of his army. The emperor himself was killed, and some ancient writers believed that as many as two-thirds of his troops fell. It was one of the greatest defeats in Roman history, and Gibbon saw it as the moment when the barbarians learned that Roman armies could be beaten in an open field.

Theodosius, who became emperor soon after the disaster at Adrianople, made peace with the Goths by allowing them to settle in the empire, and he was the last man to rule the whole Roman world. When he died in 395, the empire passed to his two sons, one of whom ruled from Constantinople and the other from Italy, and the division never really healed. The east remained wealthy and well defended, while the west, weaker and poorer, was left to face the storm.

For many years the capable general Stilicho, who was himself half Vandal by birth, defended Italy against the Gothic leader Alaric and other invaders. The young western emperor Honorius, however, was easily persuaded that Stilicho was plotting against him, and in 408 the general was executed. His death removed the last strong defender of the west, and Alaric, with little left to stop him, marched toward Rome.

In August 410, Alaric and his Goths were let into Rome through one of its gates, and for three days they plundered the city, though they spared the churches and many of its people. It was the first time in almost eight hundred years that an enemy had occupied Rome, and the shock reverberated through the entire Roman world. The emperor himself was safe in the well-defended city of Ravenna, and for the western empire the disgrace was the sign of worse to come.

At the end of 406 a mixed host of Vandals and other peoples crossed the Rhine into Gaul, and over the next years they swept through Spain. In 429 they crossed to Africa under their king Gaiseric, and in 439 they captured Carthage, the rich port from which much of Rome's grain had come. From this base the Vandals built a navy, and they became a threat to the entire western Mediterranean.

Attila, king of the Huns, whose name was already feared across Europe, led an enormous army into Gaul in 451, burning towns and demanding tribute. The Roman general Aetius joined forces with the Visigoths, and together they fought Attila to a stand-still on the Catalaunian Plains in what ancient writers described as an extremely bloody battle. The Huns withdrew from Gaul soon afterwards, but neither side could really claim to have won.

In 452 Attila invaded Italy, and a delegation led by Pope Leo met him near the river Mincio, after which the Hun king withdrew, perhaps because of sickness or lack of supplies, though tradition credited the pope. Attila died the following year, but in 455 the Vandal king Gaiseric sailed from Africa, entered Rome and plundered it for about two weeks. Pope Leo persuaded the invaders not to burn the city or to murder its inhabitants, and they spared its buildings, but the damage was severe.

In 476 a German officer named Odoacer deposed the young emperor Romulus Augustulus, a boy of about sixteen whose very name, a pair of early Roman names, seemed a bitter joke. Odoacer sent the imperial robes to the emperor in Constantinople and ruled Italy without an emperor of his own, and the boy was allowed to live in comfort. Gibbon and most later historians treat this quiet event as the end of the western empire, though many people at the time hardly noticed it.

Gibbon's most famous explanation is that the decline of Rome was the natural and inevitable result of immoderate greatness, since prosperity ripened the seeds of decay and conquest multiplied the causes of destruction. The more the empire grew, he thought, the harder it became to govern, to pay for and to defend, and the more it relied on armies that obeyed generals rather than laws. In his view, the barbarians did not so much destroy a healthy empire as push over one that was already leaning.

Gibbon blamed not only size but also the loss of civic spirit, the dominance of the army, and the rise of a new religion that turned men's attention to the hope of life after death. He famously described the story as the triumph of barbarism and religion, a phrase that has been quoted, praised and criticised ever since. Historians today still disagree about all of these causes, and many of them emphasise economics, disease and climate that Gibbon barely considered.

While the western provinces fell to invaders one by one, the eastern half of the empire survived, protected by its great capital, its strong walls and its richer economy. In 527 a vigorous, hard-working ruler named Justinian came to the throne, and beside him stood his wife Theodora, a woman of humble origins and remarkable political courage. The empire that they governed is commonly called the Byzantine Empire, though its people always called themselves Romans.

Justinian commissioned scholars to gather the vast, tangled body of Roman law into a single orderly code, a work that later shaped the legal systems of much of Europe. In the capital he also rebuilt the great church of Hagia Sophia after it was damaged in riots, and its enormous dome, completed in 537, astonished everyone who saw it. Gibbon admired the lawyers' achievement, though he thought that the emperor, for all his energy, spent too much on his buildings and wars.

Justinian dreamed of restoring the old empire, and his gifted general Belisarius conquered North Africa from the Vandals in 533 and then began the long and exhausting war to recover Italy from the Goths. Just as these ambitions seemed to be succeeding, a terrible plague reached Constantinople in 541 and spread across the Mediterranean, killing a large part of the population and weakening the empire's strength. The victories came at heavy cost, and Italy lay ravaged by war for years.

In the early seventh century the Roman and Persian empires, which had been rivals for centuries, fought a war of exceptional length and bitterness, in which the Persians at one point overran Syria and Egypt. The emperor Heraclius answered with a daring counter-attack deep into Persian territory, and in 627 he won a decisive victory near Nineveh. Both empires emerged so exhausted that neither was ready for the shock that was about to come out of Arabia.

After the death of the prophet Muhammad in 632, the armies of the new Muslim state swept out of Arabia with astonishing speed, taking Syria, Jerusalem and Egypt from the Roman Empire within about ten years. Within twenty years they had also overthrown the Persian kingdom altogether, and the empire in Constantinople was left with Anatolia, parts of Greece and some lands in Italy and North Africa. The transformation of the whole Mediterranean world that followed was one of the most dramatic in history.

Gibbon devoted several chapters to Muhammad and the rise of Islam, and he approached the subject with more curiosity and fairness than many European writers of his day. He read what translations he could find, discussed the faith and the conquests with evident interest, and acknowledged the real talents of the early leaders. His account has been criticised on points of detail by modern scholars, but it showed that a European reader could take another civilisation seriously.

On Christmas Day in the year 800, in the church of Saint Peter in Rome, Pope Leo crowned the powerful Frankish king Charlemagne as emperor of the Romans. The rulers in Constantinople, who believed that they were the only legitimate Roman emperors, regarded the ceremony as an insult, and the quarrel lingered for generations. The imperial title survived in the west, in one form or another, for about a thousand years, long after anything resembling the old empire had gone.

Gibbon often wrote with scorn about the Byzantine court, which he portrayed as a place of intrigue, flattery and empty ceremony, ruled by weak men and dangerous women. Many modern historians believe that he was unfair, since the Byzantines preserved Greek learning, produced magnificent art and defended Europe against invaders for centuries. Even so, his vivid portraits of the plotting emperors and eunuchs have remained part of the popular image of Byzantium.

In 1071 the Seljuk Turks crushed the Byzantine army at Manzikert and soon overran most of Anatolia, the heartland that had supplied the empire with soldiers and food. The emperor Alexios appealed to the Christian rulers of the west for help, and the response, a few years later, was the First Crusade, which began in 1096. The Crusaders came to recover the Holy Land, but they were often suspicious of the Byzantines, and the Byzantines, in turn, were wary of their strange and unruly allies.

In 1204 an army of the Fourth Crusade, ferried by Venetian ships and deep in debt to Venice, turned aside from its original goal and attacked the Christian city of Constantinople. The Crusaders breached the walls, plundered the city for three days and divided the empire among themselves, and many of its greatest treasures were carried off to the west. Gibbon tells the story with grim relish, and most historians agree that the empire never fully recovered from the blow.

In 1261 a Byzantine general named Michael Palaiologos recovered Constantinople from the western rulers who had held it for nearly sixty years, and he restored the empire. But what he regained was a shadow of what had been lost, with a ruined and half-empty city, a shrunken treasury and enemies pressing from every direction. For almost two more centuries, the empire survived by diplomacy, clever marriages and the strength of its enormous walls.

From about the year 1300, the Ottoman Turks, who began as a small frontier state in Anatolia, grew steadily in strength and swallowed one Byzantine province after another, until Constantinople was an island in their territory. The sultan Bayezid pressed the city hard, but in 1402 the Central Asian conqueror Timur crushed his army at Ankara, and Constantinople was granted a reprieve of about fifty years. When the Ottomans recovered from this blow, they were stronger and better organised than ever.

Mehmed the Second became sultan in 1451, a young man of great intelligence and ruthless ambition, and he resolved to take the city that had defied his ancestors. He built a fortress on the narrow strait to cut Constantinople off from the Black Sea, and he hired a gun founder named Urban, who had first offered his skills to the Byzantines, to cast an enormous bronze cannon. Against such weapons, the old walls would be tested as they never had been before.

The siege began in April 1453 with perhaps seven thousand defenders facing an Ottoman army many times larger, and the great cannon began to batter the walls day after day. The defenders had closed the harbour called the Golden Horn with a heavy chain, but Mehmed answered by having dozens of ships dragged overland on greased rollers and launched inside it. The defenders were now forced to guard a longer line, and their strength, already small, was stretched to the limit.

Before dawn on 29 May 1453, the Ottomans launched their final assault, and after hours of desperate fighting, they poured through a breach in the walls. The last emperor, Constantine the Eleventh, is said by most accounts to have thrown off his imperial robes and died fighting with his men, though his body was never certainly identified. The city that had been the capital of the eastern Roman world for more than eleven hundred years had fallen, and with it fell the last remnant of the Roman Empire.

After the conquest, Mehmed made Constantinople the capital of his own growing empire, and the great church of Hagia Sophia was turned into a mosque. The city flourished again under its new rulers, and it is now known as Istanbul, but the line of Roman emperors that began with Augustus had finally come to an end. Gibbon, whose history had covered more than a thousand years, now had reached the point at which he could close his story.

Gibbon ended his story where it had begun, among the ruins of Rome, and he recalled how the Italian scholar Poggio Bracciolini had climbed the Capitoline hill in the 1430s to look down on the shattered temples and half-buried arches. Poggio had mourned the turning of fortune's wheel, which had brought so great a city to such a state, and Gibbon, with the same feeling, wrote of the ruins that time and neglect had made. It was a fitting last page for a book about the fall of greatness.

Between eleven and twelve o'clock on the night of 27 June 1787, in a summer-house in his garden at Lausanne in Switzerland, Gibbon wrote the last lines of his history. He later said that after laying down his pen he walked up and down a covered avenue of trees beneath the moon, feeling joy at his freedom and a sober melancholy at parting from an old companion. His great work had taken nearly twenty years, and he knew that it would be the thing for which he was remembered.

The first volume appeared in 1776, and it sold out within a few weeks, delighting Gibbon and his friends and winning praise from some of the leading thinkers of the age. The second and third volumes followed in 1781, the last three in 1788, and by then he was one of the most famous writers in Europe. His polished, ironic prose and his huge footnotes were widely admired, and sentences from his work are still quoted today.

Churchmen attacked Gibbon almost at once for his treatment of early Christianity, accusing him of undermining the faith and even of mistreating his sources. He answered the sharpest of them in a pamphlet published in 1779, defending his accuracy but declining to retract anything. The controversy did his reputation no harm, since it brought his book to the attention of many readers who might otherwise never have opened it.

Modern scholars have found mistakes in Gibbon's pages, and archaeology, new documents and new methods have taught us far more than he could possibly have known. Yet they still admire the tremendous range of his reading, the care of his notes, and the independence with which he judged his sources. He remains one of the very few historians of the eighteenth century whom people read for pleasure as well as for instruction.

Many historians today prefer to describe the end of the western empire as a gradual transformation rather than a sudden collapse, in which Roman law, the Latin language and the Christian church survived inside the new barbarian kingdoms. The eastern empire, moreover, continued for nearly a thousand years after the deposition of Romulus Augustulus, and its culture shaped Greece, Russia and the Balkans. Gibbon's story of a decline remains powerful, but it is no longer the only way to read the evidence.

Gibbon died in January 1794, at the age of fifty-six, but his History has been read and argued over ever since, and it remains one of the great works of English prose. It asks a question that every generation must answer for itself, which is whether a powerful state can be undone as much by its own size, its own habits and its own divisions as by enemies at its gates. Gibbon never claimed to have the final answer, but he showed that the question was worth a lifetime of thought.
